title: Temporal Consistency Improves Generalization in Contextual Offline Meta Reinforcement Learning
claim: A task encoder feeds a latent dynamics model trained with multi-step temporal consistency, and the same latents then train the policy.
layout: 3 panels, left-to-right, shaded middle box with unrolled latent dynamics
description: A three-part left-to-right diagram. On the left, three cylinder-shaped task datasets D(1), D(2) and D(N) feed transition tuples {s, a, r, s'} into a blue trapezoid 'Context encoder E_θ', which outputs a task representation z in a light-blue box. The middle panel, inside a rounded gray box, shows an unrolled latent world model. Robot-arm observation images s0, s1 and s2 pass through red trapezoid encoders F_φ. Latent states x0 and x̂1 are advanced by the dynamics model D_φ(x, a, z), with red circles for actions a0 and a1 and rewards r0 and r1. Dotted double arrows mark the loss between predicted and target latents. On the right, a single observation passes through an encoder to a latent state x_t. It then splits into dark-gray boxes for the policy π and the value function Q. The red encoders and the robot images draw the eye first.
caption: Contextual World Model. Left: A context encoder $E_\theta$ maps transitions from each task to a task representation $z$, which serves as an implicit task identifier. Middle: An observation encoder maps observations $s_t$ to latent vectors $x_t$. A task-conditioned latent dynamics model {$D_\phi$} predicts future latent states given the current latent state, action, and task representation. The world model is trained using a classification loss based on temporal consistency. Right: An offline policy is trained using the latent states $x_t$ and task representation $z$.
abstract: Offline meta-reinforcement learning seeks to learn a policy that generalizes to new related tasks online. Context-based methods infer a task representation from transition histories, yet learning an effective task representation without supervision remains challenging. Existing methods relying on contrastive learning learn discriminative task representations, but fail to identify task-specific dynamics, while relying on reconstruction can be insufficient to model long-horizon dependencies, limiting generalization to new tasks. We investigate the impact of temporal consistency in latent space on task representation learning, showing that enforcing multi-step predictions in latent space encourages task representations that are able to capture task-dependent dynamics while preventing representation collapse. We provide theoretical analysis characterizing sources of error in value estimation and show through extensive experiments on MuJoCo, Contextual DeepMind Control, and MetaWorld benchmarks that temporal consistency significantly improves both zero-shot and few-shot generalization.
